question: Why do nontrivial 2D rotations usually have no real eigenvectors?
direct_answer: Because they rotate every nonzero direction away from itself.
expanded_answer: A nontrivial rotation changes the angle of every vector, so no real line through the origin stays fixed as a line. Since eigenvectors require a preserved direction, ordinary real eigenvectors do not exist in this case.
key_points: This is a geometric obstruction, not a computational accident
common_wrong_ideas: Thinking the axis of rotation in 2D behaves like 3D rotation axes
Believing numerical methods just fail to find them
